title: Baizhang's fox
hookLine: an old man was reborn a fox for saying the awakened are free of cause and effect (Gateless Gate 2)
last: ŌRYŌKI — CLEAN UP, EVEN AFTER INSIGHT.

lines: AN OLD MAN AT THE BACK.
cards: Every time the teacher Baizhang gave a talk, an old man stood at the back with the monks and listened. When the talk ended, he left with them. Nobody seemed to know him.
One day, when everyone else had gone, the old man stayed behind. Baizhang asked: who are you? And the old man said: I'm not a human being.
It's the second case of the Gateless Gate, and it reads like a ghost story. It's also about an old temptation in spiritual life: thinking you've gotten past the rules.

teach.b: The old man tells his story. Long ago, in the time of a Buddha before ours, I lived on this mountain as its teacher. A student asked me: does a person of great practice still fall under cause and effect?

teach.h: FIVE HUNDRED LIVES AS A FOX.
teach.b: For that answer I was reborn as a fox, five hundred lifetimes in a row. Please, give me a turning word, a phrase that can set me free.
Baizhang said: they are not blind to cause and effect. In Chinese the difference is one character. The old man had said bù luò, doesn't fall into.
Baizhang said bù mèi, isn't blind to, doesn't obscure. At that, the story says, the old man woke up.

teach.h: A MONK'S FUNERAL FOR A FOX.
teach.b: He bowed and asked Baizhang for a monk's funeral, behind the mountain. After the meal Baizhang called the monks to a funeral, and they were baffled, since no one was sick.
He led them to a rock behind the mountain, drew out a dead fox with his staff, and cremated it with full rites.
The old man thought awakening would lift him above cause and effect, the way some people imagine a spiritual person is beyond ordinary consequences. Baizhang's answer: no one is above it.
Awakening means seeing it clearly. Look back at this week. No walls, no fear.
Gone beyond. Form is emptiness. Don't solve it.
And now: even the wisest are not blind to cause.

how: Zen teachers use Baizhang's fox to warn students against thinking insight puts them beyond ethics and consequences; Baizhang himself is remembered for writing rules for monastic life.

o: a shape-shifting spirit said to haunt Chan monasteries
a nickname for a clever monk who tricked his teacher
a koan: a teacher reborn a fox for denying cause and effect

games.q: match each piece of the fox koan.
p: doesn't fall into cause and effect
five hundred lives as a fox
not blind to cause and effect
a dead fox, cremated like a monk

s: the old man said the awakened still fall under cause and effect
he said they don't, and that answer made him a fox.
Baizhang's answer changes only one Chinese character
bù luò, doesn't fall into, became bù mèi, isn't blind to.
Baizhang gave the fox a monk's funeral
he found it behind the mountain and cremated it with full rites.

games.q: a student asks you: once someone is fully awake, are they still under cause and effect? you're Baizhang. what's the turning word?
o: they aren't blind to cause and effect.
cause and effect is only an idea.
games.why: Baizhang's 'bù mèi yīnguǒ' freed the old man: awakening doesn't lift anyone above consequences, it sees them clearly.

practice: Bring to mind one small cause and its effect from today: a late night and a heavy morning, a kind word and a softer face across the table. Look at it plainly, without blame, the way you'd watch one domino tip the next.
Then watch the breath the same way, the in-breath leading to the out-breath, the out-breath making room for the next, link by link.

wordCard.voice: Baizhang's fox. An old teacher said the awakened don't fall under cause and effect, and lived five hundred lives as a fox until he heard: they aren't blind to it.

orig.note: Chinese bù mèi yīnguǒ: not blind to cause and effect, Baizhang's turning word.

carryVoice: Your line: not blind to cause. Awake doesn't mean above it. Day two hundred eighty, and the week is whole.
